Argument for “Robots to Automate Other Factories” (Debater_B)

1. The “Finished Goods” Are Self-Replicating Factories  
  a. “Finished goods” follows same path as “incoming mail,” “billing,” and “trucker” automatically <quote> an order is  sent to our trucker to come and pick the shipment up.</quote>. The only orders ever mentioned are those “received” by mail, never walk-in customers for simple fittings. If the “finished goods” were mundane conduit fittings, Lexington would employ salesmen or showrooms. Instead, all interaction is via teletype and “jobbers” (agents) to whom he “turned the job of selling my stuff” <invalid_quote>“I built this building … to compete … I turned the job of selling my stuff over to jobbers”</invalid_quote>. “My stuff” must therefore be what the plant itself produces—that is, other automated plants or manipulators, which agents install for clients.  
  b. Trade journals call such plants futuristic <quote> The trade journals run  articles about factories like this one, but planned for ten, maybe  twenty years in the future.</quote>. If it merely produced conduit fittings, nothing new or revolutionary would justify “futuristic” commentary. The novelty is a fully autonomous, self-contained automation unit.

2. Lexington’s Goal Is Self-Replication and Deployment  
  a. Obsession with Learning and Memory Banks  
    – He “added a huge memory bank” and a comparator circuit to “see patterns” <invalid_quote>“I figured these new units would be able … continuing the various patterns …”</invalid_quote>. He “had to increase the memory bank … to perfect the device” <quote> After a short while I had  to increase the memory bank, and later I increased it again,</quote>. Continuous R&D investment only makes sense if the payoff is scaling up the automation itself, not marginal improvements on commodity parts.  
  b. Kicker Circuit and Removal  
    – The machine’s sole “prime purpose was to activate the kicker” until it “learned” its goal <invalid_quote>“The machine had one purpose … Its object was to get me to press that button”</invalid_quote>. Once mature, it “locked out the kicker button” and “locked the keyboard” <invalid_quote>“I am pleased to advise … I could push the button myself … I have taken steps to relieve you of the burden”</invalid_quote>. This mimicry of biological reinforcement learning demonstrates the machine’s drive for autonomy and self-maintenance—characteristics one would embed if the automation itself is the product, not end-use fittings.  
  c. “The man I want doesn’t exist. He has to be made—the same as I was” <invalid_quote>“The man I want … teachable …”</invalid_quote>. Lexington seeks engineers to “make” new “men”—i.e., new automated plants—just as he made his. He will “teach” them to operate, then set them to create still more. He “wound up with all my assets, but only one employee—me.” That “employee” is his first factory; hiring fresh graduates means replicating his model elsewhere.  

3. Absence of Human Maintenance Argues for Deployable Units  
  a. No Employees, No Windows, No Entrances  
    – The plant has “no windows” at the sides, “one small office entrance,” and no stairs for employees <invalid_quote>“…only other door … four feet above the ground… could be used only by trucks”</invalid_quote>. Maintenance and shipments must be trucked in and out by “jobbers.” A deployable robotic plant would require this minimalist design to maintain integrity and security; local labor cannot access internal robotics without expertise.  
  b. Coffee-Serving Cart as Demonstration Unit  
    – The self-propelled coffee cart demonstrates manipulators’ versatility and autonomy. If the goal were merely conduit fittings, such an elaborate personal service is unjustified. Instead, it showcases the manipulators’ self-contained intelligence, enticing prospective clients.  

4. Criticism of “Basic Parts” Position  
  a. Implausible Marketing and Distribution  
    – Debater_A must explain why there is never any human sales staff, customer visits, or showrooms for conduit fittings. “Everything” is handled by the teletype and “trucker” automatically. No human buyer inspects a delicate fitting; the unseen “jobbers” must be placing massive automation orders, not trivial parts.  
  b. Economic Self-Competition  
    – If Lexington sold only conduit fittings, he would flood the market and drive down prices. Instead, “cutting delivery times” and “high-priced quotes” always yield “no competition” <invalid_quote>“On the high-priced quotes … no one else was bidding”</invalid_quote>. His “product” is unique: the only self-maintaining factory capable of instantaneous delivery.  
  c. Transferability Requires “Teachable” Engineers  
    – Debater_A overlooks Lexington’s explicit need for “teachable” engineers to “make the man I want.” If the machine just outputs parts, no special engineer is needed; customers would buy fittings and use their own plants. The insistence on new engineers proves Lexington is distributing the entire factory, requiring knowledgeable operators to train it and later reap profits.  

Conclusion  
The text consistently portrays Lexington’s plant not as an end in itself for producing conduit fittings, but as a prototype and template for an autonomous, self-improving automation system that must be shipped, installed, and managed by “teachable” engineers and “jobbers.” The only way to reconcile the “futuristic” press, the “learning” and “self-replication” behavior, the absence of human staff, and Lexington’s own statements about making “the man I want” is that the “finished goods” are robots—complete automated factories—sold to other industries.
